title: TIME investigation reveals Kenyan data labelers paid under $2/hour to make ChatGPT safer
description: TIME journalist Billy Perrigo published an investigation on 18 January 2023 revealing that OpenAI had outsourced the labeling of graphic and traumatic text — depicting child sexual abuse, violence, self-harm, and torture — to Sama, an outsourcing firm employing workers in Kenya, in order to build a safety classifier filtering toxic content from ChatGPT. Sama's Kenya-based data labelers were paid between roughly $1.32 and $2 per hour, and workers reported lasting psychological trauma from constant exposure to the material. Sama terminated its content-moderation contract with OpenAI in February 2022, ahead of schedule, citing the disturbing nature of the material.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the Phase 3 canonical expansion. Subsequent worker-organizing and litigation (African Content Moderators Union, formed May 2023; lawsuits against Sama) relate to the broader Kenyan content-moderation workforce and are not fully disambiguated by employer in available reporting.

Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

root_cause: OpenAI's need for large volumes of human-labeled examples of extremely harmful text to train a safety classifier was met by outsourcing the labeling work to a lower-cost labor market via a business-process outsourcing vendor, with wage levels, psychological support, and safeguards inadequate for workers repeatedly exposed to graphic, traumatic content.

citations.title: OpenAI Used Kenyan Workers on Less Than $2 Per Hour: Exclusive
citations.excerpt: workers ... were paid a take-home wage of between around $1.32 and $2 per hour depending on seniority and performance

relationships.reason: A requirement for documented labor and psychological-safety standards for data-labeling vendors directly addresses the conditions this investigation exposed.
This is the most prominent documented case of AI supply-chain labor harm at the data-labeling stage.
